name: Reading a Pinout Diagram
title: Reading a Pinout Diagram
description: A pinout diagram shows each pin's number, name, and function for a component package. Pin 1 is marked (dot, notch, or chamfer) and numbering follows the package standard - usually counterclockwise from the top view.
how_it_works: Locate pin 1 on both the diagram and the physical part, then read each pin's name and function from the datasheet table. Confirm the package variant matches - the same chip in different packages has different pinouts.
key_points: Pin 1 marked by dot, notch, or chamfer - find it first.
Numbering is usually counterclockwise viewed from the top.
Names and functions come from the datasheet table, not the diagram alone.
Package variant must match exactly - pinouts differ between packages.
requirements: Manufacturer datasheets for each component; pin numbering standard for the package; schematic symbol matching the physical pinout.
standards: IPC-7351 land patterns; JEDEC package standards (e.g., JESD30); manufacturer datasheet as authoritative source.
citations: Manufacturer datasheets (TI, Microchip, STMicroelectronics, NXP) - the authoritative pinout source.
IPC-7351B generic requirements for surface mount design and land pattern standard.

name: Power and Ground Pins
title: Power and Ground Pins
description: Power (VCC, VDD) and ground (GND, VSS) pins are the most critical connections: reversed or missing power destroys components instantly. Datasheets often show multiple power pins that must all be connected.
how_it_works: Connect every power and ground pin shown in the datasheet, add the recommended decoupling capacitors close to the pins, and verify polarity before first power-up. Never leave a power pin unconnected 'because the others are connected'.
key_points: Reversed power destroys components - verify before powering.
Connect ALL power and ground pins, not just one pair.
Place decoupling capacitors close to power pins per datasheet.
Check polarity twice; power mistakes are permanent.

name: Common Package Types

description: Pins reaching connectors (USB, buttons, sensor inputs) face electrostatic discharge and abuse. Protection devices on these pins are part of the pinout-level design.
how_it_works: Identify connector-exposed pins, add TVS diodes or protection per interface standards, and keep protection close to the connector. Test with ESD gun levels appropriate to the product's environment.
key_points: Connector pins need ESD and transient protection.
Place protection at the connector, not at the chip.
Follow interface standards for protection requirements.
Test to the environment's ESD levels.
requirements: Manufacturer datasheets for each component; pin numbering standard for the package; schematic symbol matching the physical pinout.
standards: IPC-7351 land patterns; JEDEC package standards (e.g., JESD30); manufacturer datasheet as authoritative source.
citations: Manufacturer datasheets (TI, Microchip, STMicroelectronics, NXP) - the authoritative pinout source.
IPC-7351B generic requirements for surface mount design and land pattern standard.

name: Pinout Differences Between Variants
title: Pinout Differences Between Variants

key_points: Suffixes change package, grade, and sometimes pinout.
Decode the full part number via the ordering guide.
Verify pinout for the exact variant, not the family.

name: BGA Pinouts and Fanout
title: BGA Pinouts and Fanout

how_it_works: Study the ball map, plan fanout with via-in-pad or dog-bone per manufacturer guidance, and verify the footprint against the datasheet land pattern. Simulate or carefully review high-speed BGA breakouts.
key_points: Ball maps need fanout planning before layout starts.
Via-in-pad vs dog-bone per manufacturer guidance.
Footprint must match the datasheet land pattern exactly.
Review high-speed breakouts carefully - rework is nearly impossible.

name: Connector Pinouts and Standards
title: Connector Pinouts and Standards
description: USB, HDMI, Ethernet, and power connectors have standardized pinouts - but variants (USB-C's 24 pins, PoE modes) add complexity. Wiring a connector wrong damages both ends.
how_it_works: Use the standard's pinout for the exact connector variant, verify against the datasheet, and test continuity on first articles. For custom connectors, publish your pinout as a controlled document.
key_points: Standards define connector pinouts - use the exact variant's.
Verify against datasheets; test continuity on first builds.
Custom connectors need published, controlled pinouts.
A wrong connector pinout damages both sides of the mating pair.

name: Differential Pair Pin Assignment
title: Differential Pair Pin Assignment
description: Differential signals (USB D+/D-, Ethernet pairs, LVDS) must use the pinout's designated pairs - swapping P/N or splitting pairs across the chip breaks signal integrity.
how_it_works: Assign differential signals only to their designated pin pairs, keep P/N together through the fanout, and never split a pair across distant pins. Verify polarity at both schematic and layout.
key_points: Use only designated differential pin pairs.
Keep P/N together from pin through fanout.
Verify polarity at schematic and layout stages.
Split pairs are broken pairs - route them as one.
requirements: Manufacturer datasheets for each component; pin numbering standard for the package; schematic symbol matching the physical pinout.
standards: IPC-7351 land patterns; JEDEC package standards (e.g., JESD30); manufacturer datasheet as authoritative source.

name: Reverse-Engineering Unknown Pinouts
title: Reverse-Engineering Unknown Pinouts
description: Sometimes you must determine a pinout with no datasheet - legacy parts, unmarked boards. Careful measurement (continuity, diode drops, power signatures) can recover it, with risk.

Signals by diode signatures and trace following.
Verify on a sacrificial unit before trusting.

Redundant paths for critical signals where possible.
Independent review of every pinout.
